# Section 5: KTU 2024 Scheme Examination Question Bank & Topic Recap

---

## 5.1 Part A Questions (3 Marks Each)

> **Instructions (KTU 2024):** Answer in **2–3 sentences** with a key formula. Each carries **3 marks** (2 for content, 1 for presentation).

### Q1. **[KTU University Exam – May 2024 Model Question]**
**Define Gain Margin and Phase Margin. State the conditions for stability of a closed-loop system in terms of these margins.**

**Model Answer (3 marks):**
- **Gain Margin (GM):** It is defined as the factor by which the open-loop gain can be increased before the closed-loop system reaches the verge of instability, measured at the phase crossover frequency $\omega_{pc}$. Mathematically,
  $$\text{GM}_{dB} = -20\log_{10}\vert G(j\omega_{pc})H(j\omega_{pc}) \vert$$
- **Phase Margin (PM):** It is defined as the additional phase lag that can be tolerated at the gain crossover frequency $\omega_{gc}$ before instability, given by
  $$\text{PM} = 180° + \angle G(j\omega_{gc})H(j\omega_{gc})$$
- **Stability conditions:** The closed-loop system is stable if and only if $\text{GM}_{dB} > 0$ **and** $\text{PM} > 0°$. Both conditions must be satisfied simultaneously.

---

### Q2. **[KTU University Exam – Dec 2023 Model Question]**
**What is the significance of the critical point $(-1 + j0)$ in the polar plot? What does the polar plot crossing this point imply?**

**Model Answer (3 marks):**
The point $(-1, j0)$ on the polar plot is called the **critical point** because the closed-loop characteristic equation $1 + G(s)H(s) = 0$ reduces to $G(s)H(s) = -1$ at the threshold of instability.
- If the polar plot **encircles** $(-1, j0)$ → closed-loop system is **unstable**.
- If the polar plot **passes through** $(-1, j0)$ → closed-loop system is **marginally stable** (sustained oscillations).
- If the polar plot **does not encircle** $(-1, j0)$ → closed-loop system is **stable**.

---

## 5.2 Part B Questions (14 Marks Each)

> **KTU 2024 ESE Pattern:** Each Part B question carries **14 marks** with sub-parts (typically 7 + 7). The student answers **either** Option A **or** Option B in full.

---

### **Part B – Option A** [14 Marks]
**[KTU University Exam – June 2024 Model Question]**

For a unity feedback system with open-loop transfer function
$$G(s) = \dfrac{50}{(1 + 0.1s)(1 + 2s)}$$

**Draw the polar plot and determine:**

**(a)** The gain margin and phase margin.
**(b)** Comment on the closed-loop stability.

#### Model Solution

##### Part (a) — 7 Marks

**Step 1: Substitute $s = j\omega$ and split into real/imaginary parts.**

$$G(j\omega) = \dfrac{50}{(1 + 0.1j\omega)(1 + 2j\omega)} = \dfrac{50}{(1 - 0.2\omega^2) + j(2.1\omega)}$$

Rationalize by multiplying numerator and denominator by the complex conjugate:

$$G(j\omega) = \dfrac{50\left[(1 - 0.2\omega^2) - j(2.1\omega)\right]}{(1 - 0.2\omega^2)^2 + (2.1\omega)^2}$$

**Step 2: Find Phase Crossover Frequency $\omega_{pc}$.**

$$\angle G(j\omega) = -\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{2.1\omega}{1 - 0.2\omega^2}\right) = -180°$$

This requires $1 - 0.2\omega^2 = 0$ (i.e., the denominator of the arctan is positive only for the arctan to reach $\pm 90°$, but for the angle to reach $-180°$ we need the real part of the original denominator to be zero, leading to pure imaginary denominator):

$$\boxed{\omega_{pc} = \sqrt{5} \approx 2.236\,\text{rad/s}}$$

**Step 3: Magnitude at $\omega_{pc}$.**

$$\vert G(j\omega_{pc}) \vert = \dfrac{50}{2.1 \cdot \sqrt{5}} = \dfrac{50}{2.1 \times 2.236} = \dfrac{50}{4.696} \approx 10.65$$

**Step 4: Gain Margin.**

$$\text{GM}_{dB} = 20\log_{10}\left(\dfrac{1}{10.65}\right) = 20\log_{10}(0.0939) \approx \boxed{-20.55\,\text{dB}}$$

**Step 5: Gain Crossover Frequency $\omega_{gc}$.**

Set $\vert G(j\omega_{gc}) \vert = 1$:

$$\dfrac{50}{\sqrt{(1 - 0.2\omega_{gc}^2)^2 + (2.1\omega_{gc})^2}} = 1$$

Squaring:

$$(1 - 0.2\omega^2)^2 + 4.41\omega^2 = 2500$$

$$1 - 0.4\omega^2 + 0.04\omega^4 + 4.41\omega^2 = 2500$$

$$0.04\omega^4 + 4.01\omega^2 - 2499 = 0$$

Let $x = \omega^2$:

$$0.04x^2 + 4.01x - 2499 = 0$$

Using the quadratic formula:

$$x = \dfrac{-4.01 \pm \sqrt{16.08 + 399.84}}{0.08} = \dfrac{-4.01 \pm 20.40}{0.08}$$

Taking the positive root:

$$x = \dfrac{16.39}{0.08} \approx 204.9 \quad \Longrightarrow \quad \omega_{gc} \approx 14.31\,\text{rad/s}$$

**Step 6: Phase Margin.**

$$\angle G(j\omega_{gc}) = -\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{2.1 \times 14.31}{1 - 0.2 \times 204.9}\right) = -\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{30.05}{-39.98}\right)$$

Since the real part is negative and imaginary part is positive, the angle lies in the second quadrant:

$$= -\tan^{-1}(-0.7516) = -(180° - 36.9°) = -143.1°$$

$$\text{PM} = 180° + (-143.1°) = \boxed{36.9°}$$

##### Part (b) — 7 Marks

**Stability Comment:**

- $\text{GM}_{dB} \approx -20.55\,\text{dB} < 0$ — **negative GM**
- $\text{PM} \approx 36.9° > 0$ — **positive PM**

**Verdict:** This is a **conflict case**! Although GM is negative, PM is positive. The system is **stable** in the sense that small disturbances decay, but it is **conditionally stable** with respect to gain. If the gain is increased by a factor of $\approx 10.65$ (the magnitude at $\omega_{pc}$), the system will become unstable. Therefore, the gain $K = 50$ is too high, and the system is **sensitive to gain variations**. Recommended $K_{\max} \approx 50/10.65 \approx 4.7$ for safe operation.

---

### **Part B – Option B** [14 Marks]
**[KTU University Exam – Dec 2023 Model Question]**

For a unity feedback system with open-loop transfer function
$$G(s)H(s) = \dfrac{K}{s(1 + s)(1 + 0.2s)}$$

**(a)** Sketch the Bode plot for $K = 1$ and determine the gain margin and phase margin.
**(b)** Find the value of $K$ for which the system becomes marginally stable. Find the corresponding oscillation frequency.

#### Model Solution

##### Part (a) — 7 Marks

**Step 1: Substitute $s = j\omega$ and express in Bode form.**

$$G(j\omega)H(j\omega) = \dfrac{K}{j\omega(1 + j\omega)(1 + 0.2j\omega)}$$

**Step 2: Magnitude (dB) expression for $K = 1$.**

$$\vert G(j\omega)H(j\omega) \vert_{dB} = 20\log_{10}\left(\dfrac{1}{\omega\sqrt{1 + \omega^2}\sqrt{1 + 0.04\omega^2}}\right)$$

- Initial slope: $-20\,\text{dB/dec}$ (due to $1/s$).
- At $\omega = 1$: slope changes to $-40\,\text{dB/dec}$ (corner at $\omega = 1$).
- At $\omega = 5$: slope changes to $-60\,\text{dB/dec}$ (corner at $\omega = 1/0.2 = 5$).

**Step 3: Phase expression.**

$$\angle G(j\omega)H(j\omega) = -90° - \tan^{-1}(\omega) - \tan^{-1}(0.2\omega)$$

- Starts at $-90°$ for low $\omega$.
- Goes to $-270°$ for high $\omega$.

**Step 4: Find $\omega_{pc}$ (Phase Crossover).**

Set phase = $-180°$:

$$-90° - \tan^{-1}(\omega) - \tan^{-1}(0.2\omega) = -180°$$
$$\tan^{-1}(\omega) + \tan^{-1}(0.2\omega) = 90°$$

Using the addition formula:

$$\dfrac{\omega + 0.2\omega}{1 - 0.2\omega^2} = \infty \quad \Longrightarrow \quad 1 - 0.2\omega^2 = 0$$
$$\boxed{\omega_{pc} = \sqrt{5} \approx 2.236\,\text{rad/s}}$$

**Step 5: Magnitude at $\omega_{pc}$.**

$$\vert G(j\omega_{pc})H(j\omega_{pc}) \vert = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5} \cdot \sqrt{6} \cdot \sqrt{1.2}} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{36}} = \dfrac{1}{6}$$

$$\text{GM}_{dB} = 20\log_{10}(6) \approx 15.56\,\text{dB}$$

**Step 6: Find $\omega_{gc}$ (Gain Crossover).**

Set $\vert G(j\omega_{gc})H(j\omega_{gc}) \vert = 1$:

$$\omega\sqrt{1 + \omega^2}\sqrt{1 + 0.04\omega^2} = 1$$

For small $\omega \ll 1$, the expression simplifies to approximately $\omega \cdot 1 \cdot 1 = \omega = 1$. So:

$$\omega_{gc} \approx 1\,\text{rad/s}$$ (more precisely $\omega_{gc} \approx 0.945\,\text{rad/s}$)

**Step 7: Phase Margin.**

$$\angle G(j\omega_{gc})H(j\omega_{gc}) = -90° - \tan^{-1}(0.945) - \tan^{-1}(0.2 \times 0.945)$$
$$= -90° - 43.4° - 10.7° = -144.1°$$

$$\boxed{\text{PM} = 180° + (-144.1°) = 35.9°}$$

##### Part (b) — 7 Marks

**Step 1: Marginal Stability Condition.**

The system is marginally stable when $\text{GM}_{dB} = 0$, i.e., when $\vert G(j\omega_{pc})H(j\omega_{pc}) \vert = 1$. From Step 5 of Part (a), at $\omega_{pc} = \sqrt{5}$:

$$\left\vert \dfrac{K}{j\omega_{pc}(1 + j\omega_{pc})(1 + 0.2j\omega_{pc})} \right\vert = 1$$

$$\dfrac{K}{\sqrt{5} \cdot \sqrt{6} \cdot \sqrt{1.2}} = 1 \quad \Longrightarrow \quad \dfrac{K}{6} = 1$$

$$\boxed{K_{\max} = 6}$$

**Step 2: Oscillation Frequency.**

The frequency of sustained oscillation at marginal stability is precisely $\omega_{pc}$:

$$\boxed{\omega_{osc} = \sqrt{5} \approx 2.236\,\text{rad/s}}$$

**Step 3: Verification Using Routh-Hurwitz (Optional Cross-Check).**

Characteristic equation: $s(1 + s)(1 + 0.2s) + K = 0$
$\Rightarrow s(0.2s^2 + 1.2s + 1) + K = 0$
$\Rightarrow 0.2s^3 + 1.2s^2 + s + K = 0$

Routh array:
- $s^3$: $0.2$, $1$
- $s^2$: $1.2$, $K$
- $s^1$: $\dfrac{1.2 - 0.2K}{1.2}$
- $s^0$: $K$

For marginal stability, $1.2 - 0.2K = 0 \Rightarrow K = 6$ ✓ (matches).

The auxiliary equation from $s^2$ row: $1.2s^2 + 6 = 0 \Rightarrow s^2 = -5 \Rightarrow s = \pm j\sqrt{5}$ ✓.

---

## 5.3 KTU Examiner's Valuation Warning / Pitfall Callout

> [!WARNING]
> **Common Mistakes That Cost Marks (Module 3 KTU Papers):**
>
> 1. **Sign Error in PM:** A phase angle of $-150°$ gives PM = $+30°$, **not** $-30°$. Many students write PM = $180° - \text{angle}$ (wrong) instead of $180° + \text{angle}$ (correct, because the angle is already negative).
>
> 2. **Confusing GM and PM Frequencies:** GM is read at $\omega_{pc}$ (where phase is $-180°$). PM is read at $\omega_{gc}$ (where magnitude is $0\,\text{dB}$). Mixing these up is the #1 reason students lose full marks.
>
> 3. **Forgetting Units:** GM must be reported in **dB**; PM must be reported in **degrees**. Writing "GM = 6" without "dB" loses 1 mark.
>
> 4. **DC Gain Mistake:** For Type-1 systems (one pole at origin), the polar plot starts at $\infty$ on the negative real axis. Students often incorrectly start it at the origin.
>
> 5. **Misinterpreting Negative GM:** A negative $\text{GM}_{dB}$ does **not** automatically mean the system is unstable — check the **PM** as well! A positive PM overrides a negative GM in some conditional stability cases (see Part B Option A above).
>
> 6. **Marginal vs. Absolute Stability:** In Bode plots, $\text{GM}_{dB} = 0$ and $\text{PM} = 0$ are *equivalent* conditions for marginal stability in minimum-phase systems. Always show the calculation of **both** in your answer.

---

## 5.4 Topic Recap & Important Things to Remember (Rapid Revision Checklist)

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Pre-Exam Quick-Recall (Print this section):**

- ☐ **Gain Margin (GM)** = additional gain tolerable, measured at $\omega_{pc}$ (where phase = $-180°$).
- ☐ **Phase Margin (PM)** = additional phase lag tolerable, measured at $\omega_{gc}$ (where magnitude = $0\,\text{dB}$).
- ☐ **Stability Test:** $\text{GM}_{dB} > 0$ **AND** $\text{PM} > 0°$ ⟹ **Stable**; either negative ⟹ unstable; either zero ⟹ marginal.
- ☐ **Polar Plot:** Locus of $G(j\omega)H(j\omega)$ in the complex plane as $\omega: 0 \to \infty$.
- ☐ **Critical Point:** $(-1, j0)$ — the closed-loop system is unstable if the polar plot encircles this point (for $P = 0$).
- ☐ **Bode Plot:** Two semi-log curves; magnitude in dB and phase in degrees.
- ☐ **GM in dB** = $-20 \log_{10}\vert G(j\omega_{pc})H(j\omega_{pc}) \vert$ (note the *negative* sign because we want a *positive* number when stable).
- ☐ **PM in degrees** = $180° + \angle G(j\omega_{gc})H(j\omega_{gc})$.
- ☐ **Design Targets (Bode's Rule):** $\text{PM} \approx 45°\text{–}60°$, $\text{GM} \ge 6\,\text{dB}$.
- ☐ **Minimum-phase system:** All poles and zeros in LHP. For these, $\text{GM} \approx 0 \Leftrightarrow \text{PM} \approx 0$.
- ☐ **Type-1 systems** (one pole at origin) start polar plot at $\infty$ on negative real axis at $\omega = 0^+$.
- ☐ **Marginal stability oscillation frequency** = $\omega_{pc}$ (the frequency where phase is $-180°$).
- ☐ **Maximum allowable gain** for stability = $\text{GM}$ (in linear ratio, not dB).
- ☐ **Corner frequencies** of Bode plot: $\omega_c = 1/T$ for each $(1 + Ts)$ term; for $(1 + s/a)$ form, corner is at $a$.
- ☐ **Slope changes:** Each pole adds $-20\,\text{dB/dec}$ past its corner; each zero adds $+20\,\text{dB/dec}$ past its corner.
- ☐ **Initial slope of Bode magnitude plot** = $-20 \times N$, where $N$ = system type (number of poles at origin).
- ☐ **All formulas in this topic are dimensionless in the linear sense; only the dB and degree units make the numbers human-readable.**

topics.content:
> **APJ ABDUL KALAM TECHNOLOGICAL UNIVERSITY (KTU) | 2024 SCHEME**
> - **Course:** PCAET501 - CONTROL SYSTEM THEORY
> - **Module:** Module 3
> - **Topic:** Relative Stability

<!-- SECTION_1_START -->
## 1. Core Technical Definition & Intuitive Overview

### 1.1 Formal Definition

**Relative Stability** is a quantitative measure of *how close* a closed-loop control system is to the boundary of instability. Unlike **absolute stability** (which only answers the binary question *"Is the system stable or not?"*), relative stability specifies the *degree* or *margin* of safety by which a stable system remains stable.

In the frequency domain, this margin is quantified by two principal indices defined on the open-loop transfer function $G(s)H(s)$ evaluated along the $j\omega$ axis:

- **Phase Margin (PM or $\gamma$)** — measured at the *Gain Crossover Frequency* ($\omega_{gc}$).
- **Gain Margin (GM)** — measured at the *Phase Crossover Frequency* ($\omega_{pc}$).

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **KTU 2024 Syllabus Mapping:** Relative Stability is a Module 3 topic and is **directly assessable** in Part A (3 marks: definitions) and Part B (14 marks: Bode/Nyquist-based computation of GM & PM). Mastery of this concept is essential for solving higher-order stability problems.

### 1.2 Intuitive Real-World Analogy

> [!NOTE]
> **Analogy — The Cliff Edge Walk:** Imagine a blindfolded person walking along a narrow ridge. *Absolute stability* tells you only whether they are currently on the ridge (stable) or have already fallen (unstable). *Relative stability* tells you *how far* they are from the edge of the cliff. A wider margin means they are safely in the middle of the ridge; a small margin means one wrong step and they fall.
>
> In control systems, the "cliff" is the stability boundary ($j\omega$-axis in the $s$-plane or the $(-1, j0)$ point in the Nyquist plane). **GM** and **PM** are the perpendicular distances from the open-loop frequency response to this critical point.

### 1.3 Physical Significance

- A system with **large GM and PM** is **robustly stable** — it tolerates parameter variations, component aging, and noise without becoming unstable.
- A system with **small GM and PM** is **fragile** — small disturbances or gain changes can push it into instability.
- A system with **negative GM or PM** is **unstable** under closed-loop conditions.

### 1.4 The Two Key Frequency Points

| Symbol | Name | Defining Condition on $G(j\omega)H(j\omega)$ |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| $\omega_{pc}$ | **Phase Crossover Frequency** | $\angle G(j\omega_{pc})H(j\omega_{pc}) = -180^\circ$ |
| $\omega_{gc}$ | **Gain Crossover Frequency** | $\vert G(j\omega_{gc})H(j\omega_{gc}) \vert = 1 \;\; (0\,\text{dB})$ |

These are the two critical points on the frequency response where the relative stability metrics are evaluated.

<!-- SECTION_1_END -->

<!-- SECTION_2_START -->
## 2. Deep Theoretical Analysis & KTU High-Yield Formula Sheet

### 2.1 Gain Margin (GM) — Theory

The **Gain Margin** is defined as the factor by which the open-loop gain may be increased *before* the closed-loop system becomes marginally stable (i.e., before the Nyquist plot crosses the critical point $-1 + j0$).

**Mechanism:**
1. At $\omega = \omega_{pc}$, the phase of $G(j\omega)H(j\omega)$ is exactly $-180^\circ$. This means the loop signal is inverted, so positive feedback behaviour emerges.
2. The magnitude at this frequency, $\vert G(j\omega_{pc})H(j\omega_{pc}) \vert$, indicates how strongly the system is being "pushed" towards instability.
3. If this magnitude is already $\geq 1$, the system is unstable; if it is $< 1$, the system has *gain reserve*.

**Formal Definition:**
$$GM = \frac{1}{\left\vert G(j\omega_{pc})H(j\omega_{pc}) \right\vert}$$

In decibels (the form most commonly used in Bode plots):
$$GM_{dB} = 20 \log_{10}(GM) = -20 \log_{10}\left\vert G(j\omega_{pc})H(j\omega_{pc}) \right\vert$$

**Stability Rule based on GM (for minimum-phase systems):**
- $GM_{dB} > 0 \Rightarrow$ Stable
- $GM_{dB} = 0 \Rightarrow$ Marginally stable (sustained oscillations)
- $GM_{dB} < 0 \Rightarrow$ Unstable

### 2.2 Phase Margin (PM) — Theory

The **Phase Margin** is the additional phase lag (measured in degrees) that can be introduced into the open-loop transfer function at $\omega_{gc}$ before the closed-loop system reaches the instability threshold.

**Mechanism:**
1. At $\omega = \omega_{gc}$, the magnitude is unity ($0\,\text{dB}$). Any additional phase lag will rotate the Nyquist plot further towards the $-1$ point.
2. The current phase at $\omega_{gc}$ is $\angle G(j\omega_{gc})H(j\omega_{gc})$.
3. The "available room" before the phase reaches $-180^\circ$ is the Phase Margin.

**Formal Definition:**
$$\gamma = PM = 180^\circ + \angle G(j\omega_{gc})H(j\omega_{gc})$$

**Stability Rule based on PM (for minimum-phase systems):**
- $PM > 0^\circ \Rightarrow$ Stable
- $PM = 0^\circ \Rightarrow$ Marginally stable
- $PM < 0^\circ \Rightarrow$ Unstable

### 2.3 Engineering Benchmarks (Design Heuristics)

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Designer-Standard Acceptable Ranges:**
> - **Phase Margin:** $30^\circ \leq PM \leq 60^\circ$ (the "sweet spot" is around $PM \approx 45^\circ - 60^\circ$).
> - **Gain Margin:** $GM_{dB} \geq 6\,\text{dB}$ (typical), with $GM_{dB} \geq 10\,\text{dB}$ considered very robust.
> - For a **second-order system** with damping ratio $\zeta$, the empirical relation is:
> $$\zeta \approx \frac{PM(\text{in degrees})}{100}$$
> Hence $PM = 60^\circ \implies \zeta \approx 0.6$ (a near-optimum damping for minimal overshoot and fast settling).

### 2.4 KTU Formula Sheet / Cheat Sheet

| # | Quantity | Mathematical Expression | Evaluated At | Units |
| :---: | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 1 | Phase Crossover Frequency | $\angle G(j\omega_{pc})H(j\omega_{pc}) = -180^\circ$ | — | rad/s |
| 2 | Gain Crossover Frequency | $\vert G(j\omega_{gc})H(j\omega_{gc}) \vert = 1$ | — | rad/s |
| 3 | Gain Margin (linear) | $GM = \dfrac{1}{\vert G(j\omega_{pc})H(j\omega_{pc}) \vert}$ | $\omega = \omega_{pc}$ | dimensionless |
| 4 | Gain Margin (dB) | $GM_{dB} = -20\log_{10}\vert G(j\omega_{pc})H(j\omega_{pc}) \vert$ | $\omega = \omega_{pc}$ | dB |
| 5 | Phase Margin | $\gamma = 180^\circ + \angle G(j\omega_{gc})H(j\omega_{gc})$ | $\omega = \omega_{gc}$ | degrees |
| 6 | PM vs Damping Ratio (2nd order) | $\zeta \approx PM/100$ | — | dimensionless |
| 7 | Resonant Peak $M_r$ relation | $M_r \approx \dfrac{1}{2\zeta\sqrt{1-\zeta^2}}$ for small $\zeta$ | $\omega_r$ | dimensionless |
| 8 | Bandwidth–PM relation | Higher PM $\Rightarrow$ Lower overshoot, longer settling | — | — |

### 2.5 Real-World Engineering Utility

- **Aerospace Autopilots:** Relative stability margins are mandated by aviation authorities (e.g., MIL-F-8785C requires $PM \geq 45^\circ$ and $GM \geq 6$ dB gain margin; $45^\circ$ phase margin is a typical design target for flight control laws).
- **Power Electronics Converters:** SMPS (Switched-Mode Power Supply) feedback loops are tuned using PM measured on the Bode plot of the converter's control-to-output transfer function.
- **Active Suspension Systems in Automobiles:** Adequate PM ensures passenger comfort without sustained oscillation.
- **Robotic Manipulators:** Joint controllers rely on PM to suppress vibrations and ensure smooth trajectory tracking.

<!-- SECTION_2_END -->

<!-- SECTION_3_START -->
## 3. Step-by-Step Derivations & Analytical Matrix

### 3.1 Derivation: Gain Margin from the Closed-Loop Characteristic Equation

The closed-loop characteristic equation of a unity-feedback system is:
$$1 + G(s)H(s) = 0$$

For the system to be on the verge of instability, a pair of closed-loop poles must lie exactly on the imaginary axis, i.e., $s = j\omega_{pc}$. Substituting:
$$1 + G(j\omega_{pc})H(j\omega_{pc}) = 0$$

Rearranging:
$$G(j\omega_{pc})H(j\omega_{pc}) = -1$$

This is the **critical point** in the Nyquist plot. In polar form, $-1$ has magnitude $1$ and phase $-180^\circ$ (or $+180^\circ$). Thus, the critical condition simultaneously demands:
$$\vert G(j\omega_{pc})H(j\omega_{pc}) \vert = 1 \quad \text{and} \quad \angle G(j\omega_{pc})H(j\omega_{pc}) = -180^\circ$$

This defines $\omega_{pc}$ as the frequency where the phase is exactly $-180^\circ$. At a stable operating point, the magnitude at $\omega_{pc}$ is *less* than $1$. The factor by which the gain can be multiplied (scaling $K \to K_{crit}$) to push the system onto the critical point is:
$$K_{crit} = \frac{1}{\vert G(j\omega_{pc})H(j\omega_{pc}) \vert}$$

Hence:
$$\boxed{GM = \frac{1}{\vert G(j\omega_{pc})H(j\omega_{pc}) \vert}}$$

In decibels:
$$GM_{dB} = 20 \log_{10}\!\left(\frac{1}{\vert G(j\omega_{pc})H(j\omega_{pc}) \vert}\right) = -20\log_{10}\vert G(j\omega_{pc})H(j\omega_{pc}) \vert$$

### 3.2 Derivation: Phase Margin

At the gain crossover frequency $\omega_{gc}$, the magnitude of the open-loop transfer function is unity:
$$\vert G(j\omega_{gc})H(j\omega_{gc}) \vert = 1$$

The phase at this frequency is some value $\phi = \angle G(j\omega_{gc})H(j\omega_{gc})$. If we add an additional phase lag of $\theta$ such that the total phase becomes $-180^\circ$, we have:
$$\phi - \theta = -180^\circ$$

Solving for $\theta$:
$$\theta = \phi + 180^\circ = 180^\circ + \angle G(j\omega_{gc})H(j\omega_{gc})$$

This $\theta$ is precisely the additional phase lag that destabilizes the system — and hence, by definition, the Phase Margin:
$$\boxed{\gamma = PM = 180^\circ + \angle G(j\omega_{gc})H(j\omega_{gc})}$$

### 3.3 Worked Numerical Example (Analytical Matrix)

**Problem Statement:**
For the open-loop transfer function:
$$G(s)H(s) = \frac{K}{s(s+2)(s+5)}, \quad K = 10$$

Compute the Gain Margin and Phase Margin.

---

#### Step 1: Substitute $s = j\omega$

$$G(j\omega)H(j\omega) = \frac{10}{(j\omega)(j\omega + 2)(j\omega + 5)}$$

#### Step 2: Expand the Denominator

$$(j\omega + 2)(j\omega + 5) = (j\omega)^2 + 7(j\omega) + 10 = -\omega^2 + 7j\omega + 10$$

So:
$$(j\omega)(j\omega + 2)(j\omega + 5) = j\omega \cdot (10 - \omega^2 + 7j\omega)$$

Multiplying:
$$= 10j\omega - j\omega^3 - 7\omega^2 = -\omega^3 - 7\omega^2 + 10j\omega$$

Factor out $j\omega$:
$$= j\omega(-\omega^2 - 7\omega \cdot \frac{1}{j} \cdot j + 10) \;\;\Rightarrow\;\; \text{reorganize:}$$

Let us re-expand cleanly:
$$(j\omega)(j\omega + 2)(j\omega + 5) = (j\omega)\bigl[(j\omega+2)(j\omega+5)\bigr]$$

$$(j\omega+2)(j\omega+5) = j^2\omega^2 + 7j\omega + 10 = -\omega^2 + 7j\omega + 10$$

Multiplying by $j\omega$:
$$(j\omega)(-\omega^2 + 7j\omega + 10) = -j\omega^3 + 7j^2\omega^2 + 10j\omega = -j\omega^3 - 7\omega^2 + 10j\omega$$

Grouping into real and imaginary parts:
$$= -7\omega^2 + j(10\omega - \omega^3)$$

So the real part is $-7\omega^2$ and the imaginary part is $\omega(10 - \omega^2)$.

#### Step 3: Phase of $G(j\omega)H(j\omega)$

Since the numerator $10$ is real and positive, the phase of the entire function equals the negative of the phase of the denominator:
$$\angle G(j\omega)H(j\omega) = -\tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{\text{Im(Den)}}{\text{Re(Den)}}\right) = -\tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{\omega(10-\omega^2)}{-7\omega^2}\right)$$

$$= -\tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{10 - \omega^2}{-7\omega}\right) = -\tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{\omega^2 - 10}{7\omega}\right)$$

#### Step 4: Find $\omega_{pc}$ by setting phase $= -180^\circ$

$$-\tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{\omega_{pc}^2 - 10}{7\omega_{pc}}\right) = -180^\circ$$

The arctangent reaches $-180^\circ$ when its argument is $0$ (taking the principal branch) or when the denominator is $0$ yielding a vertical asymptote. The argument becomes $0$ when:
$$\omega_{pc}^2 - 10 = 0 \;\;\Rightarrow\;\; \omega_{pc} = \sqrt{10} \approx 3.162 \text{ rad/s}$$

#### Step 5: Compute Magnitude at $\omega_{pc}$

$$\vert G(j\omega_{pc})H(j\omega_{pc}) \vert = \frac{10}{\vert j\omega_{pc} \vert \cdot \vert j\omega_{pc} + 2 \vert \cdot \vert j\omega_{pc} + 5 \vert}$$

Compute each factor:
$$\vert j\omega_{pc} \vert = \sqrt{10} \approx 3.162$$
$$\vert j\sqrt{10} + 2 \vert = \sqrt{4 + 10} = \sqrt{14} \approx 3.742$$
$$\vert j\sqrt{10} + 5 \vert = \sqrt{25 + 10} = \sqrt{35} \approx 5.916$$

Denominator product:
$$\sqrt{10} \cdot \sqrt{14} \cdot \sqrt{35} = \sqrt{10 \cdot 14 \cdot 35} = \sqrt{4900} = 70$$

Therefore:
$$\vert G(j\omega_{pc})H(j\omega_{pc}) \vert = \frac{10}{70} = \frac{1}{7} \approx 0.1429$$

#### Step 6: Compute Gain Margin

$$GM = \frac{1}{1/7} = 7 \quad \text{(linear)}$$

$$GM_{dB} = 20 \log_{10}(7) = 20 \times 0.8451 = 16.90 \text{ dB}$$

#### Step 7: Find $\omega_{gc}$ by setting magnitude $= 1$

$$\frac{10}{\omega\sqrt{\omega^2 + 4}\sqrt{\omega^2 + 25}} = 1$$

Squaring:
$$\frac{100}{\omega^2(\omega^2 + 4)(\omega^2 + 25)} = 1$$

$$\omega^2(\omega^2 + 4)(\omega^2 + 25) = 100$$

Let $x = \omega^2$:
$$x(x+4)(x+25) = 100$$
$$x(x^2 + 29x + 100) = 100$$
$$x^3 + 29x^2 + 100x - 100 = 0$$

Solving numerically (e.g., Newton-Raphson) yields $x \approx 0.9026$, so:
$$\omega_{gc} \approx \sqrt{0.9026} \approx 0.950 \text{ rad/s}$$

#### Step 8: Compute Phase at $\omega_{gc}$ and Phase Margin

$$\angle G(j\omega_{gc})H(j\omega_{gc}) = -\tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{\omega_{gc}^2 - 10}{7\omega_{gc}}\right) = -\tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{0.9026 - 10}{7 \times 0.950}\right)$$

$$= -\tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{-9.097}{6.65}\right) = -\tan^{-1}(-1.368) = -53.85^\circ$$

Therefore:
$$PM = 180^\circ + (-53.85^\circ) = +126.15^\circ$$

> [!NOTE]
> **Interpretation:** $PM = 126.15^\circ$ is *unusually large* (well above the typical $60^\circ$ design target), suggesting the system is **overdamped** and **sluggish**. $GM_{dB} = 16.90$ dB is healthy, so gain can be increased by a factor of $7$ before instability.

### 3.4 Result Tabulation

| Parameter | Value | Interpretation |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| $\omega_{pc}$ | $\sqrt{10} \approx 3.162$ rad/s | Frequency at which phase $=-180^\circ$ |
| $\omega_{gc}$ | $\approx 0.950$ rad/s | Frequency at which magnitude $= 0$ dB |
| $GM$ (linear) | $7$ | Gain can be increased $7\times$ |
| $GM_{dB}$ | $+16.90$ dB | Positive $\Rightarrow$ stable |
| $PM$ | $+126.15^\circ$ | Positive but excessive $\Rightarrow$ sluggish |

## 4. Structural Diagrams & Schematics

### 4.1 Bode Plot Architecture — Visualising PM and GM

The Bode plot is the primary engineering tool for measuring relative stability. Below is a structural flow showing how the open-loop frequency response is interpreted to extract margins.

```mermaid
graph TD
    A["Open Loop Transfer Function G of s times H of s"] --> B["Substitute s = j omega"]
    B --> C["Compute Magnitude M of omega = 20 log G of j omega H of j omega"]
    B --> D["Compute Phase phi of omega = angle G of j omega H of j omega"]
    C --> E["Locate Gain Crossover omega gc where M of omega = 0 dB"]
    D --> F["Locate Phase Crossover omega pc where phi of omega = minus 180 degrees"]
    F --> G["Read Gain Margin GM dB = minus M of omega pc"]
    E --> H["Read Phase Margin PM = 180 degrees plus phi of omega gc"]
    G --> I["Stability Verdict and Design Action"]
    H --> I
```

### 4.2 Nyquist Plot Architecture — Geometric Interpretation of PM and GM

The Nyquist plot visualizes the same data in the complex $G(j\omega)H(j\omega)$ plane. Margins correspond to *distances* to the critical $-1+j0$ point.

```mermaid
graph TD
    A["Open Loop Frequency Response G of j omega H of j omega"] --> B["Plot locus in Complex Plane"]
    B --> C["Critical Point P at minus 1 plus j0"]
    B --> D["Find Intersection with Negative Real Axis gives omega pc"]
    D --> E["Distance from Origin to Intersection = Magnitude at omega pc"]
    E --> F["GM linear = 1 divided by that magnitude"]
    B --> G["Find Intersection with Unit Circle gives omega gc"]
    G --> H["Angle of Locus at this point = phi of omega gc"]
    H --> I["PM = 180 degrees plus phi of omega gc"]
    F --> J["Relative Stability Indices"]
    I --> J
```

### 4.3 Conditional Stability Warning — A Special Case

A **conditionally stable system** has multiple $\omega_{pc}$ and $\omega_{gc}$ crossings. In such cases, a *decrease* in gain (not an increase) can destabilize the system, which violates the usual GM interpretation.

```mermaid
graph TD
    A["Conditional Stability Condition"] --> B["Multiple Phase Crossings of minus 180 degrees"]
    B --> C["Open Loop Plot Encircles minus 1 plus j0 multiple times"]
    C --> D["Increasing Gain = May Stabilize System"]
    C --> E["Decreasing Gain = May Destabilize System"]
    D --> F["Conventional GM Interpretation is Invalid"]
    E --> F
    F --> G["Use Full Nyquist Criterion and Count Encirclements"]
```

### 4.4 Standard Stability Decision Logic

```mermaid
graph TD
    Start["Compute GM dB and PM"] --> Q1{"GM dB greater than 0 dB?"}
    Q1 -- "Yes" --> Q2{"PM greater than 0 degrees?"}
    Q1 -- "No" --> Unstable["Closed Loop Unstable"]
    Q2 -- "Yes" --> Q3{"Conditional Stability?"}
    Q2 -- "No" --> Unstable
    Q3 -- "No" --> Stable["Closed Loop Stable with Positive Margins"]
    Q3 -- "Yes" --> Conditional["Margins Valid only in Operating Range"]
```

## 5. KTU 2024 Scheme Examination Question Bank & Topic Recap

### 5.1 Part A Questions (3 Marks Each)

---

**[KTU University Exam – Dec 2023]**

**Q1.** Define *Phase Margin* and *Gain Margin* as used in the frequency-domain analysis of control systems. State the stability conditions based on these margins for a minimum-phase system.

**Model Answer:**

*Phase Margin (PM, $\gamma$):* It is the additional phase lag (in degrees) that can be introduced at the gain crossover frequency $\omega_{gc}$ before the closed-loop system becomes marginally stable.

$$\gamma = 180^\circ + \angle G(j\omega_{gc})H(j\omega_{gc})$$

*Gain Margin (GM):* It is the factor by which the open-loop gain can be increased at the phase crossover frequency $\omega_{pc}$ before the system becomes marginally stable.

$$GM = \frac{1}{\vert G(j\omega_{pc})H(j\omega_{pc}) \vert}, \quad GM_{dB} = 20\log_{10}(GM)$$

*Stability conditions (minimum-phase system):* The closed-loop system is stable if and only if $GM_{dB} > 0$ dB **and** $PM > 0^\circ$.

---

**[KTU University Exam – June 2024]**

**Q2.** Differentiate between **absolute stability** and **relative stability** in control systems. Why is relative stability more informative for design engineers?

**Model Answer:**

| Aspect | Absolute Stability | Relative Stability |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Definition | Indicates only whether the system is stable or unstable | Quantifies *how stable* a stable system actually is |
| Information | Binary (yes/no) | Continuous metric (GM, PM) |
| Tools | Routh-Hurwitz, Jury, root locus | Bode plot, Nyquist plot |
| Engineering Utility | Basic pass/fail check | Design tuning of controllers |

*Engineering relevance:* A system can be absolutely stable yet have a phase margin of only $5^\circ$, making it practically unusable (large overshoot, ringing, fragile to noise). Relative stability metrics allow engineers to **quantify** robustness and **design** compensators (lead/lag/PI/PID) to achieve target margins (e.g., $PM \approx 45^\circ - 60^\circ$).

---

### 5.2 Part B Questions (14 Marks) — KTU Internal Choice Pattern

---

#### **Question A (14 Marks)** [KTU University Exam – May 2024]

**(a)** For the unity-feedback system with open-loop transfer function
$$G(s) = \frac{K}{s(s+4)(s+10)}, \quad K = 40$$
compute the **Gain Margin** in dB and the **Phase Margin** in degrees. (7 marks)

**(b)** If the gain $K$ is increased by a factor of $5$, determine the new stability status of the system. Comment on the relative stability. (7 marks)

---

**Model Solution to Q-A (a):**

**Step 1: Express $G(j\omega)$**
$$G(j\omega) = \frac{40}{j\omega(j\omega+4)(j\omega+10)}$$

**Step 2: Expand denominator**
$$(j\omega+4)(j\omega+10) = -\omega^2 + 14j\omega + 40$$
$$j\omega \cdot (-\omega^2 + 14j\omega + 40) = -j\omega^3 - 14\omega^2 + 40j\omega = -14\omega^2 + j(40\omega - \omega^3)$$

**Step 3: Phase of $G(j\omega)$**
$$\angle G(j\omega) = -\tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{40\omega - \omega^3}{-14\omega^2}\right) = -\tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{\omega^2 - 40}{14\omega}\right)$$

**Step 4: Find $\omega_{pc}$ by setting $\angle G(j\omega) = -180^\circ$**
$$\frac{\omega_{pc}^2 - 40}{14\omega_{pc}} = 0 \;\;\Rightarrow\;\; \omega_{pc}^2 = 40 \;\;\Rightarrow\;\; \omega_{pc} = \sqrt{40} = 2\sqrt{10} \approx 6.325 \text{ rad/s}$$

**Step 5: Compute magnitude at $\omega_{pc}$**
$$\vert G(j\omega_{pc}) \vert = \frac{40}{\omega_{pc}\sqrt{\omega_{pc}^2 + 16}\sqrt{\omega_{pc}^2 + 100}}$$
$$= \frac{40}{\sqrt{40}\sqrt{40+16}\sqrt{40+100}} = \frac{40}{\sqrt{40}\cdot\sqrt{56}\cdot\sqrt{140}}$$
$$= \frac{40}{\sqrt{40 \cdot 56 \cdot 140}} = \frac{40}{\sqrt{313600}} = \frac{40}{560} = \frac{1}{14}$$

**Step 6: Gain Margin**
$$GM = \frac{1}{1/14} = 14, \quad GM_{dB} = 20\log_{10}(14) = 22.92 \text{ dB}$$

**Step 7: Find $\omega_{gc}$**
$$\vert G(j\omega) \vert = 1 \;\Rightarrow\; \frac{40}{\omega\sqrt{\omega^2+16}\sqrt{\omega^2+100}} = 1$$
$$\omega^2(\omega^2+16)(\omega^2+100) = 1600$$

Let $x = \omega^2$:
$$x(x+16)(x+100) = 1600$$
$$x^3 + 116x^2 + 1600x - 1600 = 0$$

Solving numerically: $x \approx 0.928 \;\Rightarrow\; \omega_{gc} \approx 0.963$ rad/s.

**Step 8: Phase at $\omega_{gc}$**
$$\angle G(j\omega_{gc}) = -\tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{0.928 - 40}{14 \times 0.963}\right) = -\tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{-39.07}{13.48}\right) = -\tan^{-1}(-2.898) = -70.94^\circ$$

**Step 9: Phase Margin**
$$PM = 180^\circ + (-70.94^\circ) = 109.06^\circ$$

> **Result for Q-A (a):** $GM_{dB} = +22.92$ dB, $PM = +109.06^\circ$. The system is **stable with very large margins** (over-damped / sluggish).

---

**Model Solution to Q-A (b):**

New gain: $K_{new} = 5 \times 40 = 200$. The open-loop transfer function becomes:
$$G_{new}(s) = \frac{200}{s(s+4)(s+10)}$$

Since $\omega_{pc}$ depends only on phase, it is **unchanged**:
$$\omega_{pc} = 2\sqrt{10} \approx 6.325 \text{ rad/s}$$

**New magnitude at $\omega_{pc}$:**
$$\vert G_{new}(j\omega_{pc}) \vert = \frac{5 \times 40}{\text{(same denominator)}} = 5 \times \frac{1}{14} = \frac{5}{14} \approx 0.357$$

**New Gain Margin:**
$$GM_{new} = \frac{14}{5} = 2.8, \quad GM_{new, dB} = 20\log_{10}(2.8) = 8.94 \text{ dB}$$

The new $\omega_{gc}$ shifts upward (larger gain $\Rightarrow$ magnitude curve shifts up $\Rightarrow$ cross $0$ dB at higher frequency). However, since $GM_{new,dB} = +8.94 > 0$ and the phase margin will still be positive (though reduced), the system **remains stable** but with **reduced relative stability**.

> **Result for Q-A (b):** System is still stable. New $GM_{dB} \approx 8.94$ dB, $PM$ reduced. The system now lies in a more dynamic (less sluggish) operating region, closer to optimal $PM \approx 45^\circ - 60^\circ$.

---

#### **Question B (14 Marks)** [KTU University Exam – May 2024 — Alternative Choice]

**(a)** Explain the geometric construction of **Phase Margin** and **Gain Margin** on the Nyquist plot. Clearly mark the critical point $-1+j0$ and discuss what happens if the locus *passes through* this point. (7 marks)

**(b)** A unity-feedback control system has
$$G(s) = \frac{10}{s(1+0.1s)(1+0.05s)}$$
Determine the stability using the **Bode plot method** by computing the GM (in dB) and PM. Comment on the relative stability. (7 marks)

---

**Model Solution to Q-B (a):**

**Phase Margin on the Nyquist plot:** The PM is the angle between the negative real axis and the line joining the origin to the point on the locus where $\vert G(j\omega)H(j\omega) \vert = 1$ (i.e., where the locus intersects the unit circle). Equivalently, it is the angular "clearance" by which the locus at $\omega_{gc}$ stays away from the $-180^\circ$ ray passing through the critical point.

**Gain Margin on the Nyquist plot:** The GM is the *reciprocal* of the distance from the origin to the point where the Nyquist locus **crosses the negative real axis** (i.e., where the phase equals $-180^\circ$). If this crossing occurs at point $X$ on the negative real axis, then:
$$GM = \frac{1}{\vert X \vert}, \quad GM_{dB} = -20\log_{10}\vert X \vert$$

**Critical Point — Locus Passes Through $-1+j0$:** If the Nyquist locus passes *exactly* through the point $-1+j0$, then:
- $\vert G(j\omega_{pc})H(j\omega_{pc}) \vert = 1$ **and** $\angle G(j\omega_{pc})H(j\omega_{pc}) = -180^\circ$ simultaneously.
- This satisfies $1 + G(s)H(s) = 0$ at $s = j\omega_{pc}$, meaning the closed-loop characteristic equation has roots on the imaginary axis.
- The closed-loop system exhibits **sustained undamped oscillations** at frequency $\omega_{pc}$ (marginally stable).

If the locus *encircles* the $-1+j0$ point, the system is **unstable** (by the Nyquist stability criterion, the number of clockwise encirclements $N$ equals the number of RHP poles $P$, and closed-loop stability requires $N = -P$).

---

**Model Solution to Q-B (b):**

**Step 1: Substitute $s = j\omega$**
$$G(j\omega) = \frac{10}{j\omega(1+0.1j\omega)(1+0.05j\omega)}$$

**Step 2: Phase of $G(j\omega)$**
$$\angle G(j\omega) = -90^\circ - \tan^{-1}(0.1\omega) - \tan^{-1}(0.05\omega)$$

**Step 3: Find $\omega_{pc}$ (phase $= -180^\circ$)**
$$-90^\circ - \tan^{-1}(0.1\omega_{pc}) - \tan^{-1}(0.05\omega_{pc}) = -180^\circ$$
$$\tan^{-1}(0.1\omega_{pc}) + \tan^{-1}(0.05\omega_{pc}) = 90^\circ$$

The arctan sum equals $90^\circ$ when the denominators of the two arctan expressions satisfy: $\tan(A+B) = \infty$, i.e., $1 - \tan A \tan B = 0$:
$$1 - (0.1\omega_{pc})(0.05\omega_{pc}) = 0$$
$$0.005\,\omega_{pc}^2 = 1 \;\Rightarrow\; \omega_{pc} = \sqrt{200} = 10\sqrt{2} \approx 14.14 \text{ rad/s}$$

**Step 4: Magnitude at $\omega_{pc}$**
$$\vert G(j\omega_{pc}) \vert = \frac{10}{\omega_{pc}\sqrt{1+(0.1\omega_{pc})^2}\sqrt{1+(0.05\omega_{pc})^2}}$$
$$= \frac{10}{14.14 \cdot \sqrt{1+2} \cdot \sqrt{1+0.5}} = \frac{10}{14.14 \cdot \sqrt{3} \cdot \sqrt{1.5}}$$
$$= \frac{10}{14.14 \cdot 1.732 \cdot 1.225} = \frac{10}{30.0} = 0.333$$

**Step 5: Gain Margin**
$$GM = \frac{1}{0.333} = 3.0, \quad GM_{dB} = 20\log_{10}(3) = 9.54 \text{ dB}$$

**Step 6: Find $\omega_{gc}$ (magnitude $= 1$)**
$$\frac{10}{\omega\sqrt{1+0.01\omega^2}\sqrt{1+0.0025\omega^2}} = 1$$
$$\omega^2(1+0.01\omega^2)(1+0.0025\omega^2) = 100$$

Let $x = \omega^2$:
$$x(1+0.01x)(1+0.0025x) = 100$$
$$x(1 + 0.0125x + 0.000025x^2) = 100$$
$$0.000025x^3 + 0.0125x^2 + x - 100 = 0$$

Solving numerically: $x \approx 7.95 \;\Rightarrow\; \omega_{gc} \approx 2.82$ rad/s.

**Step 7: Phase at $\omega_{gc}$**
$$\angle G(j\omega_{gc}) = -90^\circ - \tan^{-1}(0.1 \times 2.82) - \tan^{-1}(0.05 \times 2.82)$$
$$= -90^\circ - \tan^{-1}(0.282) - \tan^{-1}(0.141) = -90^\circ - 15.74^\circ - 8.03^\circ = -113.77^\circ$$

**Step 8: Phase Margin**
$$PM = 180^\circ - 113.77^\circ = 66.23^\circ$$

> **Result for Q-B (b):** $GM_{dB} = +9.54$ dB, $PM \approx +66.23^\circ$.
> - $GM_{dB} > 0$ and $PM > 0$ $\Rightarrow$ **closed-loop stable**.
> - $PM = 66.23^\circ$ is **slightly above** the typical $60^\circ$ design target — **well-damped, low-overshoot response**.
> - $GM_{dB} = 9.54$ dB is **comfortable** for tolerating gain variations.
> - This is a **well-designed** control system from a relative-stability perspective.

---

### 5.3 KTU Examiner's Valuation Warning

> [!WARNING]
> **Common Pitfalls That Cost Marks (Read Carefully):**
>
> 1. **Sign error in PM formula:** Students frequently write $PM = \angle G(j\omega_{gc}) - 180^\circ$ instead of the correct $PM = 180^\circ + \angle G(j\omega_{gc})$. A negative $\angle$ (e.g., $-120^\circ$) gives $PM = 60^\circ$ — using the wrong sign yields $PM = -300^\circ$, a sign-flip that loses the entire 7 marks.
>
> 2. **Confusing $\omega_{pc}$ and $\omega_{gc}$:** The phase crossover is found by equating **phase** to $-180^\circ$, not magnitude to unity. Conversely, the gain crossover is found by equating **magnitude** to unity. Mixing these up leads to wrong GM and PM values.
>
> 3. **Forgetting to convert to dB:** GM is often required in dB. Writing the linear value $GM = 7$ without converting loses the conversion mark. Use $GM_{dB} = 20\log_{10}(GM)$.
>
> 4. **Ignoring the $\omega = \infty$ phase contribution:** For an $n$-th order system with integrator, the high-frequency phase asymptote is $-(90^\circ n + \text{type-dependent phase})$. Always verify the high-frequency phase limit.
>
> 5. **Conditional stability mis-judgement:** If the Nyquist plot crosses the negative real axis *multiple times*, the conventional "GM > 0 dB $\Rightarrow$ stable" rule breaks down. Always check for multiple encirclements of $-1+j0$ when the order exceeds 3.
>
> 6. **Not specifying units:** $PM$ must carry the degree symbol ($^\circ$); $GM$ in dB must be explicitly stated as "dB". Omitting units costs 0.5–1 mark in the KTU scheme.

---

### 5.4 Topic Recap & Important Things to Remember

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Rapid Revision Checklist — Relative Stability (Module 3)**

- **Two Margins, Two Frequencies:**
  * $\omega_{pc}$ — Phase Crossover Frequency, where $\angle G(j\omega)H(j\omega) = -180^\circ$.
  * $\omega_{gc}$ — Gain Crossover Frequency, where $\vert G(j\omega)H(j\omega) \vert = 1$ ($0$ dB).

- **Gain Margin:** $GM = 1/\vert G(j\omega_{pc})H(j\omega_{pc}) \vert$ and $GM_{dB} = 20\log_{10}(GM)$.

- **Phase Margin:** $PM = 180^\circ + \angle G(j\omega_{gc})H(j\omega_{gc})$.

- **Stability Decision (minimum-phase systems):**
  * $GM_{dB} > 0$ **and** $PM > 0^\circ$ $\Rightarrow$ **Stable**.
  * $GM_{dB} = 0$ or $PM = 0^\circ$ $\Rightarrow$ **Marginally Stable** (sustained oscillations).
  * $GM_{dB} < 0$ and $PM < 0^\circ$ $\Rightarrow$ **Unstable**.

- **Design Benchmarks:**
  * $PM \in [30^\circ, 60^\circ]$ for good transient response; $45^\circ - 60^\circ$ optimal.
  * $GM_{dB} \geq 6$ dB acceptable; $\geq 10$ dB robust.
  * $PM = 60^\circ \Rightarrow \zeta \approx 0.6$ (2nd-order approximation).

- **Special Case — Conditional Stability:** Multiple $\omega_{pc}$ crossings $\Rightarrow$ conventional GM rule may be invalid; use full Nyquist criterion (encirclement count).

- **Frequency-Domain Tools:** Bode plot (most common for PM/GM reading), Nyquist plot (geometric intuition), Nichols chart (combined $M$-circles and $N$-circles).

- **Cross-Verification:** Always cross-check GM/PM results with Routh-Hurwitz (for the exact stability boundary $K_{max}$) — they must be consistent.

- **Engineering Heuristics:** Doubling $K$ in a stable system typically *reduces* PM by ~$10^\circ$–$15^\circ$ and *increases* $GM_{dB}$ by ~$6$ dB (or vice versa, depending on the type of system). Useful for quick sanity checks.

- **Sign Convention:** Always quote PM in *positive* degrees for stable systems. A "negative PM" or "negative GM (in dB)" is the unambiguous signature of an **unstable** closed-loop system.

topics.content:
> **APJ ABDUL KALAM TECHNOLOGICAL UNIVERSITY (KTU) | 2024 SCHEME** > - **Course:** PCAET501 - CONTROL SYSTEM THEORY > - **Module:** Module 3 > - **Topic:** Gain Margin and Phase Margin # 📘 SECTION 1: Core Technical Definition & Intuitive Overview ## 1.1 Formal Academic Definition (KTU 2024 Syllabus Standard) In the frequency-domain analysis of linear time-invariant (LTI) control systems, **Gain Margin (GM)** and **Phase Margin (PM)** are the two fundamental **relative stability indices** derived from the open-loop frequency response. They quantify *how far* the system is from the **critical point $\left(-1, j0\right)$** in the **Nyquist plane** (or equivalently, its Bode plot equivalent), and are indispensable for assessing both **absolute stability** and the **quality of transient response**. > [!IMPORTANT] > **KTU 2024 Definition (Board-Standard):** > **Gain Margin (GM)** is defined as the factor by which the open-loop gain $K$ may be increased before the system reaches the verge of instability, measured at the **phase crossover frequency** $\omega_{pc}$ — the frequency at which the open-loop phase angle is $-180^\circ$ (or $-\pi$ radians). > > **Phase Margin (PM)** is defined as the additional phase lag (in degrees) that can be introduced into the open-loop transfer function at the **gain crossover frequency** $\omega_{gc}$ before the closed-loop system becomes marginally stable. --- ## 1.2 Intuitive Real-World Analogy Imagine you are **riding a bicycle** along the edge of a cliff. The bicycle is your **control system**, the cliff edge is the **instability boundary**, and your balance adjustments are the **controller corrections**. - **Phase Margin** is like asking: *"If a sudden gust of wind delays my steering by a few extra milliseconds, can I still avoid falling?"* A large PM means the system tolerates significant **phase delay** (timing errors) before losing stability. - **Gain Margin** is like asking: *"If the wind suddenly becomes twice as strong (gain doubles), can I still recover?"* A large GM means the system tolerates significant **amplification errors** before instability sets in. In engineering terms: - A **larger GM** $\Rightarrow$ system can survive a bigger **gain error** without instability. - A **larger PM** $\Rightarrow$ system can survive a bigger **time delay** without instability. > [!NOTE] > **Industry Standard Target Values (Nise, Ogata, Dorf & Bishop):** > - Acceptable design range: $\mathbf{30^\circ \le PM \le 60^\circ}$ and $\mathbf{GM \ge 6 \text{ dB}}$. > - Optimal: $\mathbf{PM \approx 45^\circ}$ to $\mathbf{60^\circ}$ for a good balance between speed of response and overshoot. --- ## 1.3 The Two Critical Frequencies Two special frequencies on the Bode/Nyquist plot define the margins: | Symbol | Name | Defining Condition | Physical Meaning | |:------:|:----:|:------------------:|:-----------------| | $\omega_{pc}$ | Phase Crossover Frequency | $\angle G(j\omega_{pc})H(j\omega_{pc}) = -180^\circ$ | Frequency where the Nyquist plot **crosses the negative real axis** | | $\omega_{gc}$ | Gain Crossover Frequency | $\vert G(j\omega_{gc})H(j\omega_{gc}) \vert = 1 \; (0 \text{ dB})$ | Frequency where the Bode **magnitude plot crosses 0 dB** | > [!TIP] > **Memory Trick for KTU Viva:** > - **"pc"** = **P**hase **C**rossover → the phase is **$-180^\circ$** (we measure **G**ain here → **GM**) > - **"gc"** = **G**ain **C**rossover → the gain is **0 dB** (we measure **P**hase here → **PM**) --- ## SECTION 1 Summary Callout > [!IMPORTANT] > **One-Line Takeaway:** GM is a **gain** measurement made where the **phase = $-180^\circ$**; PM is a **phase** measurement made where the **gain = 0 dB**. Both are measures of **distance from instability** in the frequency domain. # 📗 SECTION 2: Deep Theoretical Analysis & KTU High-Yield Formula Sheet ## 2.1 Mathematical Foundations Consider a unity-feedback closed-loop system with open-loop transfer function $G(s)H(s)$. The closed-loop system becomes **marginally stable** (i.e., poles lie on the $j\omega$-axis) when the open-loop frequency response $G(j\omega)H(j\omega)$ passes through the **critical point** $\left(-1, j0\right)$. Marginal stability occurs if and only if: $$\left\vert G(j\omega)H(j\omega) \right\vert = 1 \quad \text{AND} \quad \angle G(j\omega)H(j\omega) = -180^\circ \;( \text{or } -k\pi, \; k = 1, 3, 5, \dots)$$ This single condition splits naturally into the two margins. --- ## 2.2 Gain Margin (GM) — Step-by-Step Logic The **Gain Margin** is the reciprocal of the magnitude of $G(j\omega_{pc})H(j\omega_{pc})$: **Step 1:** Find $\omega_{pc}$ by solving the phase condition: $$\angle G(j\omega_{pc})H(j\omega_{pc}) = -180^\circ$$ **Step 2:** Compute the magnitude at this frequency: $$M_{pc} = \left\vert G(j\omega_{pc})H(j\omega_{pc}) \right\vert$$ **Step 3:** The Gain Margin is the factor by which the gain can be multiplied before instability: $$GM = \frac{1}{M_{pc}} = \frac{1}{\left\vert G(j\omega_{pc})H(j\omega_{pc}) \right\vert}$$ In **decibels** (more commonly used in Bode plots): $$GM_{dB} = 20 \log_{10}(GM) = -20 \log_{10}\left( \left\vert G(j\omega_{pc})H(j\omega_{pc}) \right\vert \right)$$ --- ## 2.3 Phase Margin (PM) — Step-by-Step Logic **Step 1:** Find $\omega_{gc}$ by solving the magnitude condition: $$\left\vert G(j\omega_{gc})H(j\omega_{gc}) \right\vert = 1$$ **Step 2:** Compute the phase angle at this frequency: $$\phi_{gc} = \angle G(j\omega_{gc})H(j\omega_{gc})$$ **Step 3:** The Phase Margin is the additional phase lag permissible before the phase reaches $-180^\circ$: $$PM = 180^\circ + \phi_{gc}$$ > [!NOTE] > The expression $180^\circ + \phi_{gc}$ is equivalent to $\left[ -(-180^\circ) - \phi_{gc} \right]$ in **signed form**, or simply the **angular gap** between the actual phase at $\omega_{gc}$ and the critical $-180^\circ$ line. --- ## 2.5 Real-World Engineering Utility | Domain | Use of GM and PM | |:-------|:-----------------| | **Aerospace (Aircraft Autopilots)** | Ensures the system remains stable despite aerodynamic gain variations with altitude and airspeed. | | **DC Motor Speed Control** | Designing PI/PID controllers using Ziegler-Nichols rules based on ultimate gain $K_u$ (related to GM). | | **Power Electronics (SMPS)** | Switching power supplies need adequate phase margin ($\approx 45^\circ$–$60^\circ$) for stable voltage regulation. | | **Robotics (Joint Actuators)** | High PM ensures smooth motion without oscillatory jerks. | | **Process Control (Chemical Plants)** | Conservative PMs ($45^\circ$–$60^\circ$) are mandated to account for plant parameter drift. | > [!TIP] > **Why margins matter in industry:** They give a **robustness** measure — guaranteeing stability even if the **mathematical model** of the plant differs from the **real plant** by up to the margin amount. This is the practical heart of **robust control**. # 📕 SECTION 3: Step-by-Step Derivations & Analytical Matrix ## 3.1 Exhaustive Derivation of GM and PM from the Characteristic Equation Consider a unity-feedback closed-loop system with open-loop transfer function: $$G(s)H(s) = \frac{K \cdot N(s)}{D(s)}$$ The **closed-loop characteristic equation** is: $$1 + G(s)H(s) = 0 \;\;\Longrightarrow\;\; D(s) + K \cdot N(s) = 0$$ **At the verge of instability**, the characteristic equation has roots on the $j\omega$-axis. Substitute $s = j\omega$: $$1 + G(j\omega)H(j\omega) = 0 \;\;\Longrightarrow\;\; G(j\omega)H(j\omega) = -1$$ Splitting this complex equality into its real and imaginary parts (or equivalently, magnitude and phase): $$\left\vert G(j\omega)H(j\omega) \right\vert \cdot e^{j\angle G(j\omega)H(j\omega)} = 1 \cdot e^{-j180^\circ}$$ Equating magnitude: $$\left\vert G(j\omega)H(j\omega) \right\vert = 1 \quad \quad \text{(condition for PM)} \quad \cdots (i)$$ Equating phase: $$\angle G(j\omega)H(j\omega) = -180^\circ \quad \quad \text{(condition for GM)} \quad \cdots (ii)$$ These are exactly the definitions of $\omega_{gc}$ and $\omega_{pc}$ respectively. --- ## 3.2 Worked Numerical Example 1 (Standard 2nd-Order System) > **Problem:** For $G(s)H(s) = \dfrac{K}{s(s+2)}$, determine the GM and PM for $K = 2$. **Step 1 — Substitute $s = j\omega$:** $$G(j\omega)H(j\omega) = \frac{K}{j\omega(j\omega+2)} = \frac{K}{j\omega \cdot j\omega + 2j\omega} = \frac{K}{-(\omega^2) + j2\omega}$$ Rearranging: $$G(j\omega)H(j\omega) = \frac{K}{-\omega^2 + j2\omega}$$ **Step 2 — Magnitude:** $$\left\vert G(j\omega)H(j\omega) \right\vert = \frac{K}{\sqrt{(-\omega^2)^2 + (2\omega)^2}} = \frac{K}{\sqrt{\omega^4 + 4\omega^2}} = \frac{K}{\omega\sqrt{\omega^2 + 4}}$$ **Step 3 — Phase:** $$\angle G(j\omega)H(j\omega) = - \tan^{-1}\left(\frac{2\omega}{-\omega^2}\right)$$ The denominator is negative for all $\omega > 0$, so we are in the 2nd quadrant: $$\angle G(j\omega)H(j\omega) = -180^\circ + \tan^{-1}\left(\frac{2\omega}{\omega^2}\right) = -180^\circ + \tan^{-1}\left(\frac{2}{\omega}\right)$$ **Step 4 — Find $\omega_{pc}$ (phase = $-180^\circ$):** $$-180^\circ + \tan^{-1}\left(\frac{2}{\omega_{pc}}\right) = -180^\circ \;\;\Longrightarrow\;\; \tan^{-1}\left(\frac{2}{\omega_{pc}}\right) = 0^\circ \;\;\Longrightarrow\;\; \omega_{pc} \to \infty$$ Since $\omega_{pc} = \infty$, the magnitude at $\omega_{pc}$ is: $$\left\vert G(j\omega)H(j\omega) \right\vert_{\omega \to \infty} = \lim_{\omega \to \infty} \frac{K}{\omega\sqrt{\omega^2 + 4}} = 0$$ **Step 5 — Compute GM:** $$GM = \frac{1}{0} = \infty \quad (\text{or } + \infty \text{ dB})$$ **Step 6 — Find $\omega_{gc}$ (magnitude = 1):** $$\frac{K}{\omega_{gc}\sqrt{\omega_{gc}^2 + 4}} = 1 \;\;\Longrightarrow\;\; K = \omega_{gc}\sqrt{\omega_{gc}^2 + 4}$$ Squaring both sides: $$K^2 = \omega_{gc}^2 \left(\omega_{gc}^2 + 4\right) = \omega_{gc}^4 + 4\omega_{gc}^2$$ For $K = 2$: $$4 = \omega_{gc}^4 + 4\omega_{gc}^2$$ Let $x = \omega_{gc}^2$: $$x^2 + 4x - 4 = 0$$ Using the quadratic formula: $$x = \frac{-4 \pm \sqrt{16 + 16}}{2} = \frac{-4 \pm \sqrt{32}}{2} = \frac{-4 \pm 4\sqrt{2}}{2} = -2 \pm 2\sqrt{2}$$ Taking the positive root: $$x = \omega_{gc}^2 = -2 + 2\sqrt{2} = 2(\sqrt{2} - 1) \approx 0.8284$$ $$\omega_{gc} = \sqrt{0.8284} \approx 0.9102 \text{ rad/s}$$ **Step 7 — Phase at $\omega_{gc}$:** $$\angle G(j\omega_{gc})H(j\omega_{gc}) = -180^\circ + \tan^{-1}\left(\frac{2}{0.9102}\right) = -180^\circ + \tan^{-1}(2.197)$$ $$\angle G(j\omega_{gc})H(j\omega_{gc}) = -180^\circ + 65.53^\circ = -114.47^\circ$$ **Step 8 — Compute PM:** $$PM = 180^\circ + (-114.47^\circ) = 65.53^\circ$$ **Final Answer:** $$\boxed{\omega_{gc} \approx 0.91 \text{ rad/s},\quad PM \approx 65.53^\circ,\quad GM = \infty}$$ > [!NOTE] > **Physical Interpretation:** The infinite GM is a feature of **Type-1 (or higher)** systems where the Nyquist plot starts at infinity along the negative imaginary axis as $\omega \to 0^+$, so it never crosses the negative real axis. Type-0 systems can have finite GM. --- ## 3.3 Worked Numerical Example 2 (Type-0 System with Finite GM) > **Problem:** $G(s)H(s) = \dfrac{K}{(s+1)(s+5)}$. Compute GM and PM for $K = 10$. **Step 1 — Substitute $s = j\omega$:** $$G(j\omega)H(j\omega) = \frac{K}{(j\omega+1)(j\omega+5)}$$ Expanding the denominator: $$(j\omega+1)(j\omega+5) = j^2\omega^2 + 5j\omega + j\omega + 5 = -\omega^2 + 5 + j6\omega = (5 - \omega^2) + j6\omega$$ **Step 2 — Phase condition for $\omega_{pc}$:** $$\angle G(j\omega_{pc})H(j\omega_{pc}) = -\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{6\omega_{pc}}{5 - \omega_{pc}^2}\right) = -180^\circ$$ For the arctan to yield $180^\circ$, the denominator must be negative and the ratio infinite: $$5 - \omega_{pc}^2 < 0 \;\;\Longrightarrow\;\; \omega_{pc}^2 > 5 \;\;\Longrightarrow\;\; \omega_{pc} > \sqrt{5}$$ $$\frac{6\omega_{pc}}{5 - \omega_{pc}^2} \to \pm \infty \;\;\text{when}\;\; 5 - \omega_{pc}^2 = 0 \;\;\Longrightarrow\;\; \omega_{pc} = \sqrt{5} \text{ rad/s}$$ **Step 3 — Magnitude at $\omega_{pc} = \sqrt{5}$:** $$\left\vert G(j\omega_{pc})H(j\omega_{pc}) \right\vert = \frac{K}{\sqrt{(5 - \omega_{pc}^2)^2 + (6\omega_{pc})^2}} = \frac{K}{\sqrt{0 + (6\sqrt{5})^2}} = \frac{K}{6\sqrt{5}}$$ For $K = 10$: $$\left\vert G(j\omega_{pc})H(j\omega_{pc}) \right\vert = \frac{10}{6\sqrt{5}} = \frac{10}{13.416} \approx 0.7454$$ **Step 4 — Gain Margin:** $$GM = \frac{1}{0.7454} = 1.342 \quad \Rightarrow \quad GM_{dB} = 20\log_{10}(1.342) \approx 2.56 \text{ dB}$$ **Step 5 — Find $\omega_{gc}$ (magnitude = 1):** $$\frac{K^2}{(5 - \omega^2)^2 + 36\omega^2} = 1$$ $$(5 - \omega^2)^2 + 36\omega^2 = K^2 = 100$$ $$25 - 10\omega^2 + \omega^4 + 36\omega^2 = 100$$ $$\omega^4 + 26\omega^2 - 75 = 0$$ Let $y = \omega^2$: $$y^2 + 26y - 75 = 0$$ $$y = \frac{-26 \pm \sqrt{676 + 300}}{2} = \frac{-26 \pm \sqrt{976}}{2} = \frac{-26 \pm 31.24}{2}$$ Taking the positive root: $$y = \frac{5.24}{2} = 2.62 \;\;\Longrightarrow\;\; \omega_{gc} = \sqrt{2.62} \approx 1.619 \text{ rad/s}$$ **Step 6 — Phase at $\omega_{gc}$:** $$\angle G(j\omega_{gc})H(j\omega_{gc}) = -\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{6 \times 1.619}{5 - 2.62}\right) = -\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{9.714}{2.38}\right) = -\tan^{-1}(4.082)$$ $$\angle G(j\omega_{gc})H(j\omega_{gc}) = -76.22^\circ$$ **Step 7 — Phase Margin:** $$PM = 180^\circ - 76.22^\circ = 103.78^\circ$$ > [!NOTE] > A very large PM ($> 90^\circ$) usually indicates an **over-damped, slow** closed-loop response. A more typical target is $45^\circ$–$60^\circ$. --- ## 3.4 Analytical Matrix — Interpretation of Results | Result Combination | Stability Status | Engineering Interpretation | |:-------------------|:-----------------|:---------------------------| | $GM_{dB} > 0$ dB **and** $PM > 0^\circ$ | ✅ **Stable** | System is robustly stable. | | $GM_{dB} = 0$ dB **or** $PM = 0^\circ$ | ⚠️ **Marginally Stable** | Sustained oscillations at $\omega_{pc}$ or $\omega_{gc}$. | | $GM_{dB} < 0$ dB **or** $PM < 0^\circ$ | ❌ **Unstable** | Closed-loop poles in the right-half plane. | | Large $GM$ but small $PM$ | Unstable / Marginal | The system is sensitive to **phase delays** (time lag). | | Small $GM$ but large $PM$ | Unstable / Marginal | The system is sensitive to **gain errors**. | | Both $GM$ and $PM$ large | **Very Robust** | Conservative design — may be **over-damped** and **slow**. | | $PM = 45^\circ$ to $60^\circ$ | **Optimal Trade-off** | Best balance: low overshoot, fast settling. | # 📙 SECTION 4: Structural Diagrams & Schematics ## 4.1 Conceptual Block Diagram — How GM and PM Are Measured ```mermaid flowchart TD A[Open-Loop Transfer Function GsHs] --> B[Evaluate Frequency Response Gj omega H j omega] B --> C{Identify Critical Frequencies} C --> D[Phase Crossover omega_pc

Mention the standard accepted ranges for a well-designed system.** **Model Answer:** **Gain Margin (GM):** It is defined as the factor by which the open-loop gain $K$ of the system can be increased before the closed-loop system reaches the verge of instability. Mathematically, $$GM = \frac{1}{\left\vert G(j\omega_{pc})H(j\omega_{pc}) \right\vert} \quad \text{or} \quad GM_{dB} = 20\log_{10}(GM)$$ where $\omega_{pc}$ is the phase crossover frequency at which $\angle G(j\omega_{pc})H(j\omega_{pc}) = -180^\circ$. **Phase Margin (PM):** It is the additional phase lag (in degrees) that can be introduced into the open-loop transfer function at the gain crossover frequency $\omega_{gc}$ before the system becomes marginally stable. $$PM = 180^\circ + \angle G(j\omega_{gc})H(j\omega_{gc})$$ **Standard Accepted Ranges:** - Phase Margin: $30^\circ \le PM \le 60^\circ$ (optimal: $\approx 45^\circ$–$60^\circ$) - Gain Margin: $GM_{dB} \ge 6$ dB *(3 marks — KTU rubric: 1 mark each for GM and PM definition, 1 mark for ranges)* --- ### Q2. **[KTU University Exam — Dec 2023, Model]** **Distinguish between Gain Crossover Frequency ($\omega_{gc}$) and Phase Crossover Frequency ($\omega_{pc}$). What is the significance of these frequencies in stability analysis?** **Model Answer:** | Feature | Gain Crossover Frequency ($\omega_{gc}$) | Phase Crossover Frequency ($\omega_{pc}$) | |:--------|:--------------------------------------:|:----------------------------------------:| | Defining condition | $\vert G(j\omega)H(j\omega) \vert = 1$ (0 dB) | $\angle G(j\omega)H(j\omega) = -180^\circ$ | | Read on Bode plot | Where the magnitude curve crosses 0 dB | Where the phase curve crosses $-180^\circ$ | | Used to compute | **Phase Margin (PM)** | **Gain Margin (GM)** | | Geometric meaning on Nyquist plot | Intersection with **unit circle** | Intersection with **negative real axis** | **Significance:** A system is stable if and only if the Nyquist plot encircles the critical point $\left(-1, j0\right)$ an appropriate number of times. The proximity of $\omega_{gc}$ and $\omega_{pc}$ to this critical point (captured by GM and PM) provides a quantitative measure of **relative stability** — how robust the system is to parameter variations. *(3 marks — KTU rubric: 2 marks for distinction, 1 mark for significance)* --- ## 5.2 Part B — ESE Long-Answer Questions (Internal Choice) ### 🔹 Question A (14 Marks) — **[KTU University Exam — May 2024 Pattern]** **For the unity feedback system with open-loop transfer function $G(s)H(s) = \dfrac{10}{s(s+2)(s+5)}$, determine:** **(a)** The phase crossover frequency $\omega_{pc}$ and the gain margin $GM$ in dB. **(b)** The gain crossover frequency $\omega_{gc}$ and the phase margin $PM$ in degrees. Comment on the stability of the system. --- #### **Solution to Part (a) — 7 Marks** **Step 1:** Replace $s$ with $j\omega$: $$G(j\omega)H(j\omega) = \frac{10}{j\omega(j\omega+2)(j\omega+5)}$$ **Step 2:** Find the angle of the denominator. Let us expand $(j\omega+2)(j\omega+5)$: $$(j\omega+2)(j\omega+5) = j^2\omega^2 + 5j\omega + 2j\omega + 10 = (10 - \omega^2) + j7\omega$$ So: $$G(j\omega)H(j\omega) = \frac{10}{j\omega \cdot \left[(10 - \omega^2) + j7\omega\right]} = \frac{10}{j\omega(10 - \omega^2) - 7\omega^2}$$ $$= \frac{10}{-7\omega^2 + j\omega(10 - \omega^2)}$$ **Step 3:** Phase of the system: $$\angle G(j\omega)H(j\omega) = -\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{\omega(10 - \omega^2)}{-7\omega^2}\right)$$ For the phase to equal $-180^\circ$, the denominator must be negative and the ratio must tend to $\pm\infty$: $$-7\omega^2 < 0 \;\;\text{(true for all }\omega > 0\text{)}$$ The phase equals $-180^\circ$ when: $$\omega(10 - \omega^2) = 0 \;\;\Longrightarrow\;\; \omega = 0 \text{ or } \omega^2 = 10 \;\;\Longrightarrow\;\; \omega_{pc} = \sqrt{10} \approx 3.162 \text{ rad/s}$$ We discard $\omega = 0$ (degenerate). So $\omega_{pc} = \sqrt{10}$ rad/s. **Step 4:** Magnitude at $\omega_{pc} = \sqrt{10}$: $$\left\vert G(j\omega_{pc})H(j\omega_{pc}) \right\vert = \frac{10}{\omega_{pc} \cdot \sqrt{(10 - \omega_{pc}^2)^2 + (7\omega_{pc})^2}}$$ At $\omega_{pc} = \sqrt{10}$, we have $10 - \omega_{pc}^2 = 0$, so: $$\left\vert G(j\omega_{pc})H(j\omega_{pc}) \right\vert = \frac{10}{\sqrt{10} \cdot \sqrt{0 + (7\sqrt{10})^2}} = \frac{10}{\sqrt{10} \cdot 7\sqrt{10}} = \frac{10}{7 \cdot 10} = \frac{1}{7}$$ **Step 5:** Compute $GM$: $$GM = \frac{1}{1/7} = 7 \quad \text{(linear)}, \quad GM_{dB} = 20\log_{10}(7) = 20 \times 0.8451 \approx 16.9 \text{ dB}$$ *(7 marks — 2 for setup, 2 for $\omega_{pc}$, 2 for magnitude, 1 for GM)* --- #### **Solution to Part (b) — 7 Marks** **Step 1:** Solve the magnitude condition $\left\vert G(j\omega_{gc})H(j\omega_{gc}) \right\vert = 1$: $$\frac{100}{\omega_{gc}^2 \left[(10 - \omega_{gc}^2)^2 + 49\omega_{gc}^2\right]} = 1$$ $$\omega_{gc}^2 \left[(10 - \omega_{gc}^2)^2 + 49\omega_{gc}^2\right] = 100$$ Let $u = \omega_{gc}^2$: $$u \left[(10 - u)^2 + 49u\right] = 100$$ $$u \left[100 - 20u + u^2 + 49u\right] = 100$$ $$u \left[u^2 + 29u + 100\right] = 100$$ $$u^3 + 29u^2 + 100u - 100 = 0$$ Solving numerically (using trial): $u = 0.957$ works approximately. Check: $0.957^3 + 29(0.957^2) + 100(0.957) - 100 = 0.876 + 26.555 + 95.7 - 100 = 23.13$ — too high. Try $u = 0.5$: $0.125 + 7.25 + 50 - 100 = -42.6$. So root lies between 0.5 and 0.957. Try $u = 0.85$: $0.614 + 20.95 + 85 - 100 = 6.57$. Try $u = 0.8$: $0.512 + 18.56 + 80 - 100 = -0.928$. Try $u = 0.81$: $0.531 + 19.04 + 81 - 100 = 0.571$. So $u \approx 0.805$, hence: $$\omega_{gc} \approx \sqrt{0.805} \approx 0.897 \text{ rad/s}$$ **Step 2:** Phase at $\omega_{gc} = 0.897$: $$\angle G(j\omega_{gc})H(j\omega_{gc}) = -90^\circ - \tan^{-1}\left(\frac{\omega_{gc}}{2}\right) - \tan^{-1}\left(\frac{\omega_{gc}}{5}\right)$$ $$= -90^\circ - \tan^{-1}(0.4485) - \tan^{-1}(0.1794)$$ $$= -90^\circ - 24.16^\circ - 10.18^\circ = -124.34^\circ$$ **Step 3:** Phase Margin: $$PM = 180^\circ - 124.34^\circ = 55.66^\circ$$ **Stability Comment:** Since $GM_{dB} = 16.9$ dB $> 0$ dB and $PM = 55.66^\circ > 0^\circ$, the closed-loop system is **stable** with **good relative stability** (PM is in the optimal range of $30^\circ$–$60^\circ$). *(7 marks — 3 for $\omega_{gc}$ calculation, 2 for phase at $\omega_{gc}$, 1 for PM, 1 for stability comment)* --- ### 🔹 Question B (14 Marks) — Alternative Choice **[KTU University Exam — Dec 2023 Pattern]** **For a unity feedback control system with open-loop transfer function $G(s)H(s) = \dfrac{K(1 + 0.5s)}{s(1 + s)(1 + 0.2s)}$:** **(a)** Determine the value of $K$ such that the phase margin is $45^\circ$. Find the corresponding gain margin. **(b)** For the value of $K$ found in part (a), determine the gain crossover frequency and comment on the closed-loop stability. --- #### **Solution to Part (a) — 7 Marks** **Step 1:** Open-loop frequency response: $$G(j\omega)H(j\omega) = \frac{K(1 + j0.5\omega)}{j\omega(1 + j\omega)(1 + j0.2\omega)}$$ **Step 2:** Magnitude: $$\left\vert G(j\omega)H(j\omega) \right\vert = \frac{K\sqrt{1 + 0.25\omega^2}}{\omega\sqrt{1 + \omega^2}\sqrt{1 + 0.04\omega^2}}$$ **Step 3:** Phase: $$\phi(\omega) = \tan^{-1}(0.5\omega) - 90^\circ - \tan^{-1}(\omega) - \tan^{-1}(0.2\omega)$$ **Step 4:** Apply the PM = $45^\circ$ condition. The phase at $\omega_{gc}$ is: $$\phi(\omega_{gc}) = -180^\circ + 45^\circ = -135^\circ$$ So: $$\tan^{-1}(0.5\omega_{gc}) - 90^\circ - \tan^{-1}(\omega_{gc}) - \tan^{-1}(0.2\omega_{gc}) = -135^\circ$$ $$\tan^{-1}(0.5\omega_{gc}) - \tan^{-1}(\omega_{gc}) - \tan^{-1}(0.2\omega_{gc}) = -45^\circ$$ Take tangent on both sides. Using the identity $\tan(A - B) = \dfrac{\tan A - \tan B}{1 + \tan A \tan B}$: Let $A = \tan^{-1}(\omega_{gc})$ and $B = \tan^{-1}(0.2\omega_{gc})$, then $A + B = \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{\omega_{gc} + 0.2\omega_{gc}}{1 - 0.2\omega_{gc}^2}\right) = \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1.2\omega_{gc}}{1 - 0.2\omega_{gc}^2}\right)$. The equation becomes: $$\tan^{-1}(0.5\omega_{gc}) - \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1.2\omega_{gc}}{1 - 0.2\omega_{gc}^2}\right) = -45^\circ$$ Using $\tan(A - B)$ formula and equating to $\tan(-45^\circ) = -1$: $$\dfrac{0.5\omega_{gc} - \dfrac{1.2\omega_{gc}}{1 - 0.2\omega_{gc}^2}}{1 + 0.5\omega_{gc} \cdot \dfrac{1.2\omega_{gc}}{1 - 0.2\omega_{gc}^2}} = -1$$ Let $u = \omega_{gc}^2$ for simplification. Cross-multiplying and simplifying (algebraic steps omitted for brevity but should be shown in exam) yields the polynomial: $$0.1u^2 + 1.1u - 1.2 = 0 \;\;\Longrightarrow\;\; u^2 + 11u - 12 = 0$$ Using the quadratic formula: $$u = \frac{-11 \pm \sqrt{121 + 48}}{2} = \frac{-11 \pm 13}{2}$$ Taking the positive root: $u = 1 \;\;\Longrightarrow\;\; \omega_{gc} = 1$ rad/s. **Step 5:** Find $K$ using the magnitude condition at $\omega_{gc} = 1$: $$\left\vert G(j1)H(j1) \right\vert = \frac{K\sqrt{1 + 0.25}}{\sqrt{1} \cdot \sqrt{2} \cdot \sqrt{1.04}} = 1$$ $$K = \frac{\sqrt{2} \cdot \sqrt{1.04}}{\sqrt{1.25}} = \frac{1.4142 \times 1.0198}{1.1180} = \frac{1.4422}{1.1180} \approx 1.29$$ **Step 6:** Find $\omega_{pc}$ for gain margin: $$\phi(\omega_{pc}) = -180^\circ$$ $$\tan^{-1}(0.5\omega_{pc}) - 90^\circ - \tan^{-1}(\omega_{pc}) - \tan^{-1}(0.2\omega_{pc}) = -180^\circ$$ $$\tan^{-1}(0.5\omega_{pc}) - \tan^{-1}(\omega_{pc}) - \tan^{-1}(0.2\omega_{pc}) = -90^\circ$$ This requires the argument inside the combined arctan to be infinite. Numerical solution gives $\omega_{pc} \approx 1.5$ rad/s. **Step 7:** Magnitude at $\omega_{pc} = 1.5$ rad/s: $$\left\vert G(j1.5)H(j1.5) \right\vert = \frac{1.29 \times \sqrt{1 + 0.5625}}{1.5 \times \sqrt{1 + 2.25} \times \sqrt{1 + 0.09}} = \frac{1.29 \times 1.25}{1.5 \times 1.803 \times 1.044}$$ $$= \frac{1.6125}{2.823} \approx 0.571$$ **Step 8:** Gain Margin: $$GM = \frac{1}{0.571} = 1.75 \quad \Rightarrow \quad GM_{dB} = 20\log_{10}(1.75) \approx 4.86 \text{ dB}$$ *(7 marks — 3 for finding $\omega_{gc}$, 2 for $K$ calculation, 2 for GM)* --- #### **Solution to Part (b) — 7 Marks** **Step 1:** With $K = 1.29$ and $\omega_{gc} = 1$ rad/s, verify stability: - $GM_{dB} = 4.86$ dB $> 0$ dB → **stable by gain margin criterion** - $PM = 45^\circ > 0^\circ$ → **stable by phase margin criterion** **Step 2:** Closed-loop characteristic equation: $$1 + G(s)H(s) = 0$$ $$s(1+s)(1+0.2s) + 1.29(1+0.5s) = 0$$ $$s(1 + 1.2s + 0.2s^2) + 1.29 + 0.645s = 0$$ $$0.2s^3 + 1.2s^2 + s + 0.645s + 1.29 = 0$$ $$0.2s^3 + 1.2s^2 + 1.645s + 1.29 = 0$$ **Step 3:** Routh-Hurwitz check: $$\begin{array}{c|cc} s^3 & 0.2 & 1.645 \\ s^2 & 1.2 & 1.29 \\ s^1 & \frac{1.2 \times 1.645 - 0.2 \times 1.29}{1.2} = \frac{1.974 - 0.258}{1.2} = 1.43 & 0 \\ s^0 & 1.29 & \end{array}$$ All first-column elements ($0.2, 1.2, 1.43, 1.29$) are positive → **no sign changes → closed-loop system is STABLE.** **Stability Comment:** The system is **stable with a moderate gain margin and phase margin**. While the system is theoretically stable, the GM of 4.86 dB is below the recommended 6 dB, suggesting it has limited robustness to gain variations. The PM of $45^\circ$ is at the lower end of the acceptable range, indicating moderate transient response with some overshoot. *(7 marks — 2 for Routh array setup, 3 for computation, 2 for stability comment and interpretation)* --- > [!WARNING] > **🚨 KTU Examiner's Valuation Warning — Common Mark-Loss Pitfalls:** > 1. **Unit confusion:** Always state GM in BOTH linear and dB forms; PM in degrees (or radians with explicit unit). > 2. **Sign error in PM formula:** PM = $180^\circ + \phi_{gc}$ — do NOT write PM = $180^\circ - \phi_{gc}$. The phase is negative, so adding the magnitude works. > 3. **$\omega_{pc}$ for Type-1 systems:** Many students forget that for systems with integrators, $\omega_{pc} \to \infty$ and GM = $\infty$. This is correct — do not artificially find a finite value. > 4. **Skipping units:** $\omega_{gc}$ and $\omega_{pc}$ must be in **rad/s**. Lose 0.5 mark if missing. > 5. **Stability verdict without numerical values:** Always quote numerical GM (dB) and PM ($^\circ$) values before concluding. --- ## 5.3 📌 Topic Recap & Important Things to Remember (Rapid Revision Checklist) - ✅ **GM** = factor by which gain can be increased before instability; measured at $\omega_{pc}$ (where phase = $-180^\circ$). - ✅ **PM** = extra phase lag tolerable; measured at $\omega_{gc}$ (where magnitude = 0 dB). - ✅ **GM formula (linear):** $GM = \dfrac{1}{\vert G(j\omega_{pc})H(j\omega_{pc}) \vert}$ - ✅ **GM formula (dB):** $GM_{dB} = 20\log_{10}(GM) = -20\log_{10}(\vert G(j\omega_{pc})H(j\omega_{pc}) \vert)$ - ✅ **PM formula:** $PM = 180^\circ + \angle G(j\omega_{gc})H(j\omega_{gc})$ - ✅ **Stability:** $GM > 1$ (or $GM_{dB} > 0$ dB) **AND** $PM > 0^\circ$ → STABLE. - ✅ **Optimal design:** $PM \approx 45^\circ$–$60^\circ$, $GM_{dB} \ge 6$ dB. - ✅ **Type-1 and higher systems** usually have **infinite GM** (Nyquist plot never crosses the negative real axis). - ✅ **Type-0 systems** can have **finite GM** (Nyquist plot starts on the negative real axis at $\omega = 0^+$). - ✅ **Approximate relation (2nd-order only):** $\zeta \approx \dfrac{PM \text{ (in deg)}}{100}$ and $M_r \approx \dfrac{1}{\sin(PM)}$. - ✅ **For Nyquist plot:** GM = distance from origin to negative real axis crossing (reciprocal); PM = angular distance from negative real axis to unit circle crossing. - ✅ **For Bode plot:** GM is a **vertical distance** (in dB) below the 0 dB line at $\omega_{pc}$; PM is a **horizontal/angular distance** (in degrees) above the $-180^\circ$ line at $\omega_{gc}$. - ✅ **GM and PM are independent** — knowing one does NOT automatically give the other for higher-order systems. - ✅ **Higher-order systems** are usually designed using the **dominant pole approximation** to apply 2nd-order PM-overshoot relations. - ✅ **Remember:** Negative PM or GM ⇒ UNSTABLE. Zero PM or GM ⇒ MARGINALLY STABLE (sustained oscillations).
